html:
A group of ruined Hindu temples in a mountain valley in Quảng Nam province, central Vietnam, built by the kings of Champa from about the 4th to the 13th century. It was the religious heart of the Cham kingdoms.

The first temple, built of wood by King Bhadravarman for the god Shiva, burned down and was rebuilt in brick in the 7th century. Later kings added towers for some nine centuries, each in red brick with sandstone carving, so the site works as a record of Cham art over time. The royal capital lay nearby at Trà Kiệu, and kings were honoured here as forms of the god.

Mỹ Sơn is often set beside Angkor and Prambanan as one of the great Hindu sites of Southeast Asia, though it is far smaller. Champa slowly lost ground to Đại Việt and the site was forgotten until French scholars studied it around 1900. Many of the towers were destroyed by American bombing in 1969 during the Vietnam War. UNESCO listed the site in 1999.
sum: A group of ruined Hindu temples in a mountain valley in Quảng Nam province, central Vietnam, built by the kings of Champa from about the 4th to the 13th century. It was the religious heart of the Cham kingdoms.
